<reason>A (CON) argued with genuine originality — the law/bargain distinction, "imputed consent," and the coverage-statistic critique were crisp and memorable, and A honestly answered B's pressure question with a real alternative (public floor plus client liability). But B (PRO) controlled the frame from the first rebuttal: A's opening conceded "minimum standards can be honest and general," and B converted the entire debate into "which kind of floor." On that terrain A's core offense boomeranged — rigidity, imposition without consent, and pricing out marginal firms all apply at least as much to A's own uniform statutory minimum, and B said so cleanly and repeatedly ([B2.1], [B4.1], the calibration dilemma at [B4.4], and the closing's "a floor blunt enough to satisfy CON's honesty protects nobody well"). A's best surviving point — incumbent capture of classification and schedules — stayed alive but was asserted more than comparatively developed, and A's coverage answer arrived only under pressure, partially conceding B's premise that the uniform number alone never reaches the outsourced worker. B weighed more explicitly, answered both pressure questions directly with turns rather than dodges, and made the debate easier to decide on the motion's own "across entire industries" terms.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1]: capturing A's concession that general minimums are honest, then reversing the rigidity critique onto the uniform statutory floor — restructuring the debate into "what kind of imposition," where A's attacks mostly indicted A's own alternative. Reinforced by [B4.4]'s dilemma: a floor high enough to matter carries job risk, one low enough to be riskless protects nobody, and only industry-level negotiation calibrates — a move A never squarely escaped.</best_rebuttal>
